sentences.text: Coelophysis ranks among the earliest known dinosaur genera, characterized by a lightly built frame that reached lengths of up to 3 meters and heights exceeding one meter at the hips.
Its skull featured an elongated snout with large openings to reduce weight, while its legs contained hollow bones, a trait reflected in the generic name Coelophysis.
A Coelophysis skull from the Carnegie Museum of Natural History became the second dinosaur to travel to space, flying aboard the Space Shuttle Endeavour on January 22, 1998.
This species is also notable as one of the oldest dinosaurs for which the presence of feathers has been suggested.
It holds the distinction of being the official state fossil of New Mexico, with the specific species C. bauri designated to this honor in 1981.
Edward Drinker Cope originally placed the type species in the genus Coelurus in 1887 before describing it as Coelophysis bauri in 1889, naming it after Georg Baur.
Excavations at the Ghost Ranch quarry continued through 1947 and 1948, yielding hundreds of skeletons that were classified as a single species, marking the greatest Triassic find in North America.
As a predator, Coelophysis possessed blade-like, recurved, and finely serrated teeth on both edges, with approximately 26 teeth in the upper jaw and 27 in the lower.
Evidence of cannibalism was found in specimen NMMNH P-44551, which contained regurgitated material including fragments of juvenile teeth and jaw bones.
Researchers suggest the large congregation of individuals at Ghost Ranch may have gathered to feed or drink, while similar findings in Zimbabwe imply the animal was gregarious.
Variation in proportions suggests the existence of robust and gracile morphs, with estimated weights of 15 kg for the gracile form and 20 kg for the robust form.
The animal likely reached sexual maturity between its second and third year, attaining a full length of just over 10 feet by its eighth year, and females laid clutches of 24 to 26 eggs.
The tail's lattice structure may have helped the animal maneuver at high speeds.
Research indicates that Coelophysis lived in floodplain environments with distinct dry and wet seasons.
Research in 2026 reconstructed the optimal jumping performance of C. bauri as similar to that of the elegant crested tinamou.
It is debated whether Megapnosaurus was once a species within Coelophysis, but it is now considered a valid genus.

Some researchers debate the validity of Coelophysis as a distinct genus, suggesting it is a metataxon lacking unique characteristics, yet it was designated a nomen conservandum to resolve taxonomic confusion.
Independent work by Sterling Nesbitt, Randall Irmis, and William Parker in 2007 upheld the identification of Eucoelophysis as a silesaurid, distant from Coelophysis.
Coelophysis fossils from Ghost Ranch were found in the Chinle Formation, which was believed to be of Norian age at the time of discovery.

Hunt and Lucas argued that Coelophysis lived in the Revueltian-age Petrified Forest Formation, while C. rhodesiensis fossils have been recovered from the Upper Elliot Formation in South Africa and the Forest Sandstone Formation in Zimbabwe.
